newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian politicians unite to condemn racism.
newsitem.headline: Australian politicians unite to condemn racism.

text.p: Australia's government and opposition united on Wednesday to condemn racial prejudice as a divisive and politically painful national debate on racism and immigration rumbled on.

Facing a mounting backlash from Asia and growing criticism at home over the race row, Prime Minister John Howard accepted a Labor opposition proposal for a joint parliamentary motion condemning racism and pledging tolerance.

"This motion, it is about saying to the Australian people and saying to the nations of the region that we are a tolerant society, we are a compassionate society..." Howard said in moving the motion, which was carried by a large majority.
"It is also a statement of some fundamental beliefs about the nature of our existence as human beings in Australia."
The motion said the lower house "denounces racial intolerance in any form as incompatible with the kind of society we want to be".

It also reaffirmed the right of all Australians to be "treated with equal respect regardless of race, colour, creed or origin," and "reaffirms its commmitment to maintaining Australia as a culturally diverse, tolerant and open society".
Asian newspapers have criticised Howard for failing to take a tough stand against outspoken independent politician Pauline Hanson, who sparked the race debate.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Wednesday he had written to the Bangkok-based newspaper The Nation rejecting as "inaccurate and offensive" an editorial headlined "Howard's silence endorses Australia's racist fringe".

But embarrassing incidents continued. Police in Queensland state said they were investigating two assaults on visiting Singaporean soldiers, although they did not think the attacks had been racially motivated. One case also involved robbery.

Hanson, from conservative northern Queensland state, complained in her maiden parliamentary speech last month that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for an immediate halt to immigration.

A magazine poll published on Wednesday said two out of three Australians backed her anti-immigration stand and a Hanson-led political party would win an influential bloc of parliamentary seats. Hanson was absent for Wednesday's parliamentary debate.
Her comments have been blamed for a rise in incidents of racial abuse and a sharp increase in official complaints of racism to the human rights commission.
"I, for one, haven't been very proud to be an Australian the last few weeks," deputy opposition leader Gareth Evans, a former foreign minister, told parliament.
Malaysian High Commissioner Dato Adnan Othman told reporters that there was no reason why the race debate should affect his country's relationship with Australia.
"As far as we are concerned, we do not want to have this issue blown up out of all proportion. It certainly should not affect in any way our bilateral relationship," he said.
Howard's conservative Liberal-National government, while condemning racism, has defended Hanson's right to speak out and has blamed the racism controversy on the media.
Howard told parliament Australia, with a large and diverse mix of immigrants, was one of the world's most tolerant nations.

"There are few nations in the world that can boast such a record of democracy, such a record of fair treatment and such a record of harmoniously blending together of people of different racial backgrounds than Australia," he said.
